The ISPS Code is structured in two parts:

• Part A sets out mandatory requirements, including the obligation for port facilities to

conduct a Port Facility Security Assessment and to develop, implement, and maintain

an approved Port Facility Security Plan. The latter defines measures to prevent, detect,

and respond to security threats affecting port infrastructure, operations, personnel,

and cargo.

• Part B provides non-mandatory guidance on how to meet the requirements of Part A,

including illustrative examples of risks and mitigation measures.

Despite its broad governance scope, the ISPS Code was designed primarily to address

physical security risks and has undergone only limited updates since its adoption.

Cybersecurity is not included among the mandatory requirements in Part A. References

Box 8 Case studies: Delivery and communication styles of cybersecurity

training methods

The Port of Antwerp-Bruges demonstrated the importance of training delivery methods

by using creative approaches, including organizing a Cybersecurity Escape Room and

cybersecurity-focused shows. While these initiatives require significant effort, lower-intensity

measures can also be highly effective. For example, inviting a speaker from a company that has

experienced a cyber incident has proven successful in raising employee awareness.

Maintaining continuous awareness requires ongoing communication, not just periodic

training events. The Gambia Ports Authority, for instance, sends weekly warning emails to

staff highlighting social engineering threats such as phishing, helping to keep security

top-of-mind throughout the year.
